title: 4 things great subject leaders know and do
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart notes that teachers often become subject leaders as soon as induction ends, with no leadership training, and that the role can be a career opportunity in a school with good systems or a thankless task without them. Drawing on excellent subject leaders he has worked with, he sets out four things they know and do. First, they understand the reasoning behind content choice and sequencing, which protects curriculum coherence when units are questioned or changed. Second, they preserve the discipline of their subject so that it does not shrink to a list of facts or dissolve into generic topic work. Third, they identify and champion the subject's active ingredients, such as concrete, pictorial and abstract representations in maths, giving consistency without prescribing every method. Fourth, they build trust through supportive conversations and subtle early quality assurance before formal observation, and they use subject champions to spread new practice.
points: Strong subject leaders know why content is sequenced as it is, so they can adapt a published scheme for local relevance without breaking its coherence.
They guard the subject's own ways of knowing, so pupils and staff understand what it means to learn history or science, whether or not teaching is topic based.
Defining a few conceptual active ingredients, rather than mandating tools like Numicon, gives consistency while keeping teacher autonomy and avoids cargo cult teaching.
Informal expertise, such as noticing worksheets at the photocopier and starting a conversation, builds credibility long before any observation.
Leaders who rush into lesson observation too early damage trust, whereas those who are invited in have earned it.
quotes: Leading a subject is a tough job. ITT prepares teachers to teach but as soon as the induction period is completed, teachers often take on the leadership of a subject without any sort of training.

When they receive feedback from staff about a unit of work not quite working out or a colleague suggests an alternative, they know each unit’s part in the grand scheme and the knock on effects of subsequent conceptual development if a unit were to be changed. This knowledge helps to preserve the the curriculum’s coherence.

It is this knowledge that prevents a cargo cult approach to the teaching of a subject. They ingredients are conceptual, guiding teachers of different aged children to focus on what makes a difference while affording autonomy of how they are applied.

Getting this balance right gives the consistency that some senior leaders crave without threatening autonomy. It is also a key driver in reducing the variability of teaching across the school, Clear active ingredients, understood by everyone is a way to ensure that there is alignment in what leaders have committed to in terms of great teaching.
Sometimes subject leaders move too quickly into more formal quality assurance and end up trying to observe lessons too soon.

They take the time to build their credibility with supportive conversations before they get anywhere near something that might be perceived as an observation. In the best examples, they get invited in when colleagues see that they have expertise – a great example of building trust while getting the important work of school improvement done.
